Moth and Gravel. Field Note 16.
The number got better. An AI

narrated edition of the
published note.

A room full of computers is
doing its work. Fans turn, water

moves. Somewhere above the room,
a number gets better. It would

make a reassuring green tile. We
open the account underneath it.

2 hours from the same week. The
material is a public record from

the Energy Systems Integration
Facility. 5 power channels, a

published efficiency ratio, and
a separate weather file. Strewen

Clark and Justin Strelka
published the data set through

what is now the National
Laboratory of the Rockies. We

pinned the source files and kept
1 week, the 14th to the 20th of

July 2025, open on the bench. 2
hours in that week make a useful

pair. During the first, the
facility's estimated mean demand

is 2.683 MW. During the second,
it is 2.953 MW. Demand rises by

10.077% The period efficiency
ratio falls from 1.063015

Source clock hours. Energy
estimated from recorded power.

Account A. The 14th of July,
2300 to the following midnight.
Facility energy 2682.661 kWh.

IT energy 2523.635 kWh. Period
PUE

Account B. The 18th of July,
9:00 to 10:00. Facility energy

2952.992 kWh. IT energy 2804.
.529 kWh.

Period PUE 1.052937. PUE is
facility energy divided by IT

energy. A smaller overhead
relative to IT can sit beside a

larger absolute load. Both
numbers can be right. Nothing in

these 2 hours tells us that 1
caused the other. We have no

account of useful computing
work, no controlled

intervention, and no grounds to
call 1 hour a better service.

The pair shows why 1 ratio
cannot carry the whole account.

Keep the units attached. The
file contains power in

kilowatts. Energy needs time. We
treat each reported power as a

point sample. The publisher does
not specify the instrument's

averaging window. Between
neighboring readings, we draw a

straight line, clip it at the
hour boundary, and integrate the

trapezoid underneath it. The
result is an estimate in

kilowatt hours. Every component
uses the same valid intervals.

Missing or negative components
leave time uncovered. A gap over

90 seconds also stays uncovered.
We do not fill silence with zero

demand. The selected week has
complete coverage under that

rule. The larger archive has
missing values and outlying

ratios worth inspecting. The
hourly ratio divides the two

energy totals. Averaging the
sample ratios would answer

another question. It produces a
nearby number here, but

proximity is a poor reason to
lose the definition. The

publisher's time stamps carry no
time zone. We preserve their

clock, including microseconds,
without quietly turning it into

finished time. Weather is
matched only to an earlier

reading on that same source
clock within 90 seconds. The

alignment of the two
instruments' clocks remains

unverified. A room with its own
label. We wanted somewhere to

look while keeping that account
in view. A graphite cabinet

door, a water connection above
it, a working light reflected in

the floor. The room is authored
in meters, with constructed

racks, server faces, valves, and
overhead services. Its lighting

and surfaces can be inspected.
Selecting a system opens its

facility level meter boundary
beside the geometry. The data

does not tell us how many racks
to draw, where they stood, or

what each consumed. The room
makes no such claim. Its

geometry remains an
interpretation. The account

remains recorded. More
convincing materials should make

that distinction easier to read,
not easier to overlook. A

reserve is a choice. A separate
branch lets the recorded hour

meet a chosen grid cap and
battery. At the second hour

demand, a 2.5 MW cap leaves work
for the reserve. A 500 kWh

battery starts at 80%, keeps 10%
in reserve, and delivers 92% of

the energy it discharges. With
the branch's 1 MW output limit,

it supplies 322 kWh. Conversion
loss is 28 kWh. The remaining

accounting shortfall is about
130.992 kWh. Those assumptions

are ours. They model neither a
generator starting nor a server

failing. There is no cooling
response, charging, or workload

rescheduling hidden behind the
button. Change a choice, and the

branch must be calculated again.
Export it, and the assumptions

travel with it. A useful number
should be able to make that

journey from a reassuring tile,
through its arithmetic, back to

what was observed, and what
somebody chose. Method, sources,

limits. What this account can
support. Source. Clark and

Strelka. ESIF Facility PUE data
set. DOI 10.779/3015212.

Credit, DOE/ NREL/ Alliance.
Source use implies no

endorsement. The complete
publisher notice accompanies the

extract and every exported
inspection. The replay retains

10,080 observations and 1 power
observation on either side of

the week for boundary
interpolation. Every hour covers

3,600 seconds under the stated
validity rule. JavaScript energy

integrals are checked against a
separate Python implementation

using 50 digit decimal
arithmetic. This checks

numerical implementation, not
meter calibration. No

calibration uncertainty was
supplied. The publisher's

measurement boundaries include
attributed shared loads. We use

the published channels without
adding that allowance again.

Undocumented heat reuse fields
stay raw. We derive no heat

recovery quantity from them. For
the larger question, Berkeley

Lab's 2025 DOE data center load
flexibility workshop summary and

LUMI's job energy accounting
limits describe different

boundaries around flexibility
and workload energy. Neither

supplies measurements for this
room. Inspect the source hashes

and numerical method. Complete
publisher notice. You have been

listening to Moth and Gravel
Field Notes. The written edition
is at mothandgravel.com.
